briefs.working_title: Why You See More Bugs After a Pest Control Treatment
briefs.primary_kw: seeing more bugs after pest control
secondary_kws: dead roaches after pest control treatment
how long after pest control do bugs go away
briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: a homeowner sees more insects, or large roaches dead or slow on the floor, in the days after a pest control visit and asks whether the treatment worked)
briefs.thesis: Seeing insects in the days after a pest control visit does not by itself mean the treatment failed, and which insect you see decides what it means. UF/IFAS says the ideal ant bait is slow-acting so that the ants share it with the colony, and that ants that cross an outdoor barrier treatment do not die at once and may be found dead indoors. UF/IFAS says the large roaches people call palmetto bugs are generally outdoor insects that do not survive well indoors, while the small German cockroach lives and breeds indoors and is a different problem. Do not spray over the treatment, give it the time the pest needs, and call when the signs in this post say it is not settling.
outline: The short answer: seeing insects after a visit is common and usually settles; what we tell our own customers is that activity should fall off over the following days to a couple of weeks, depending on the pest; what it means depends on which insect it is, so the post covers ants, the large outdoor roaches and the small German cockroach in turn, then what not to do and the signs that mean you should call

Ants: why bait can mean more ants at first: UF/IFAS says the ideal ant bait holds a slow-acting ingredient that does not repel ants, mixed into a food they prefer; because ants feed each other, the bait reaches the other members of the colony, including the queen and brood; that is why ants crowding a bait placement in the first days are doing what the bait needs them to do, and our own prep guide tells customers they may see more ants for a few days; UF/IFAS also says that ants that cross an outdoor barrier treatment do not die immediately and that their bodies may be found inside the home, and that ants may start foraging indoors again once that barrier wears off

Large roaches (palmetto bugs) after a treatment: UF/IFAS says the larger cockroaches (American, Australian, brown and smokybrown) are often called palmetto bugs, are generally found outdoors, and become an indoor problem when they migrate or are carried in; outdoor cockroaches do not survive well indoors, and UF/IFAS says removing them from the house is often all that is needed; the American cockroach lives outside and wanders in for food and water or to get out of extreme weather, coming from sewers through the plumbing and from trees and shrubs beside the building or with branches over the roof; UF/IFAS calls the Australian cockroach the most common cockroach found outdoors in southern Florida; so one large roach on the floor more often points to the outdoors and to how it got in than to roaches breeding in the kitchen; UF/IFAS also says the Australian cockroach can survive indoors in subtropical areas when it is cold, so large roaches seen indoors again and again are worth a call (link /pest-control/cockroach-types-southwest-florida/)

Small roaches in the kitchen or bathroom need a different plan: UF/IFAS says the German cockroach is usually found in the kitchen and bathroom, does not enter from outdoors, and is spread by people; a German cockroach treatment is judged over weeks: UF/IFAS says insect growth regulators need four to six weeks for a noticeable decrease, and that with a growth regulator you should expect to see more cockroaches during the day, which means that treatment is working; UF/IFAS also says surface and baseboard sprays do not give full control of cockroaches quickly; the statements about growth regulators apply only when a treatment included one, so ask your provider what yours included (link /pest-control/tiny-cockroach/ and /pest-control/how-long-to-get-rid-of-cockroaches/)

What not to do while a treatment works: do not spray store-bought insecticide on the insects you see or near any bait: UF/IFAS says sprays are repellent and that if they contaminate ant bait the ants will not eat it, and says never to spray a liquid insecticide where cockroach baits have been applied because it repels cockroaches from the bait; keep crumbs, grease and open food cleaned up, because UF/IFAS says food sources compete with cockroach baits and make them less effective; light cleaning is fine, but our prep guide asks customers not to wipe baseboards, hinges and treated cracks and corners for a couple of weeks

Signs that it is not settling, and when to call: small roaches in the kitchen or bathroom at any time; UF/IFAS says German cockroaches seen in the open during the daytime point to a large population that will need more than one control tactic, and that all life stages together (adults, nymphs and egg cases) point to an established infestation; activity that has not fallen off after a couple of weeks, which is the span we give our own customers; before you call, write down what you saw, in which room and at what time of day, because that tells a technician which pest it is and where it comes from

Make the house harder to enter: UF/IFAS says to pull mulch away from the house, because the large outdoor cockroaches breed prolifically in pine straw mulch and poorly in gravel or on bare soil; door thresholds should fit tightly, since a space the width of a quarter is enough for a cockroach to enter, and a simple check is to stand inside and look for light around the doors; UF/IFAS says cockroaches often come indoors during dry periods because they are looking for moisture, so fix leaks; EPA advises anyone who hires pest control to ask the company to find and correct the source of the problem before it applies pesticides (link /pest-control/garage-door-seal-roaches-parrish-fl/)

What Waves does and does not do: we tell customers what to expect after a visit, as described above; recurring WaveGuard plans include unlimited callbacks between scheduled visits at no extra charge, so a plan customer who still sees activity can ask for a return visit (link /waveguard-memberships/ and /pest-control/what-to-expect-pest-control-visit/); activity inside from German cockroaches is handled as its own treatment with follow-up visits, not as part of a regular exterior service; to have a home looked at, request a pest control quote; call to action: link "Request a Pest Control Quote" to /pest-control-quote/

briefs.working_title: Roaches, Ants or Spiders in Your Car: A Southwest Florida Guide
briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: drivers found roaches, ants or small spiders in a car, one of them in a clean car, and asked how they got there and what to do)
briefs.thesis: Insects in a car are mostly a carried-in problem, and the fix is cleaning and finding the source, not a fogger. UF/IFAS says German cockroaches are spread entirely by people, in things such as grocery bags, book bags and purses, and that food particles attract ants. UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County reports brown widow spiders making a home in cars and RVs. EPA says total release foggers should not be used in small, enclosed places. University and agency pest pages are written for buildings and say little about cars, so this post says plainly where it applies building guidance to a car.
outline: The short answer: find out which insect it is; take out food, drink containers, bags and clutter; vacuum the whole interior; do not set off a fogger in a car; if small roaches keep turning up, the home or workplace the car travels between needs a look too

What is known about bugs in cars, and what is not: the university and agency pest pages we read are written for homes and other buildings; none of them says that cockroaches or ants nest or breed in cars; what they do say explains how insects get into a car and what removes them, and the post says so each time it applies building guidance to a car

Roaches in a car: UF/IFAS says German cockroaches do not enter structures from outdoors, are spread entirely by humans and live only in association with people; they can first infest a home when infested grocery bags are brought inside, children can carry them from school in book bags and lunch containers, and people can carry them on backpacks, purses and clothing; EPA says to check packages and boxes for pests before carrying them into your home; a car that moves those same bags and boxes is one more place they can ride, so small roaches in a car are a reason to check where the car has been (link /pest-control/tiny-cockroach/ and /pest-control/get-rid-of-german-cockroaches/); a single large roach is different: UF/IFAS says the larger cockroaches are generally found outdoors

Ants in a car: UF/IFAS says any type of food or food particles can attract and provide food for ants, and calls cleanliness the best approach to ant control in the home; UF/IFAS describes ghost ants as opportunistic nesters in places that sometimes stay habitable for only a few days or weeks, says they will nest in potted plants, and says that in Florida the ghost ant is mostly found from Sarasota to Orlando and south; so crumbs, sweet spills and plants or bags carried in the car are the first things to check; the UF/IFAS ant pages we read do not mention ants nesting in vehicles (link /pest-control/tiny-ant-identification-florida/)

Small spiders in a car: do not guess the species; UF/IFAS says spiders are mostly nonaggressive, shy and generally not a threat to humans, and that the only spiders native to or established in Florida with medically significant venom are the widow spiders; UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County says complaints about brown widow spiders in cars and RVs indicate that this spider will make a home there, that the brown widow is the widow species people most often find around homes and workplaces in Sarasota County, and that widow spiders are generally non-aggressive and retreat when disturbed; the same page says bites usually happen when a spider is pressed against the skin, for example when a hand goes into a recessed area or dark corner, and that gloves should be worn if you suspect widow spiders are present; anyone bitten who feels unwell should contact a doctor (link /pest-control/spider-identification/)

Clean first: EPA says clutter gives pests places to breed and hide and makes it hard to get rid of them, so empty the car of wrappers, drink containers, bags and stored items; vacuum seats, floor, console, door pockets, child seats and trunk; UF/IFAS says a vacuum removes cockroaches immediately, and UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County says a thorough vacuuming removes spiders, their egg sacs and webbing; both statements were written for buildings, and the same tool is the practical one for a car; wipe up sticky spills, since food particles are what attract ants

Do not use a fogger in a car: EPA says the aerosol propellants in total release foggers typically are flammable and that improper use may cause a fire or explosion; EPA says foggers should not be used in small, enclosed places such as closets, cabinets, or under counters or tables, and that use of a fogger in an enclosed space may cause the product to explode; EPA's list does not name vehicles, but a car interior is a small enclosed space; a CDC report on illnesses and injuries related to total release foggers in 10 states from 2007 to 2015 counted vehicles as the most common of the other exposure locations, with 21 cases; UF/IFAS adds that the effect of cockroach foggers is limited to the cockroaches that directly contact the fog

What Waves does and does not do: Waves treats cars, trucks and vans for German cockroaches, and a car can be treated as part of a home German cockroach treatment; the vehicle service on our list is for German cockroaches, so for ants or spiders in a car the cleaning steps above come first; if roaches are in the home as well, request a pest control quote so the home and the car are handled together (link /pest-control-services/); call to action: link "Request a Pest Control Quote" to /pest-control-quote/

briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: customers ask what to clean before a German cockroach treatment, what they may clean afterward, and whether the house cleaner can come)
briefs.thesis: Cleaning is part of a German cockroach treatment, before and after. UF/IFAS says to use sanitation before and at the same time as chemical control: grease makes treatments less effective, droppings hold the scent that draws cockroaches back, and crumbs and cardboard feed and shelter them. After a Waves treatment, our prep guide says normal counter and dish cleanup is fine once everything is dry, dead roaches and droppings are vacuumed after a week, and three things are left alone: the bait placements, the monitors, and store-bought sprays. The post keeps two kinds of statement apart: what UF/IFAS, EPA and CDC say, and what our own prep guide asks Waves customers to do.
outline: The short answer: before the visit, cut the grease, crumbs, clutter and cardboard; after a Waves visit, our prep guide says normal counter and dish cleanup is fine once everything is dry, dead roaches and droppings wait a week before they are vacuumed, and the bait placements and monitors stay where they are, with store-bought sprays left on the shelf; a house cleaner can keep coming if they know those rules; if another company treated your home, follow its instructions

Why cleaning is part of the treatment: UF/IFAS says to use prevention and sanitation methods before and at the same time as chemical control; greasy surfaces decrease the effectiveness of insecticide applications; scrubbing cockroach droppings away with hot, soapy water reduces the aggregation pheromone that attracts cockroaches to the area; on food, give both UF/IFAS statements: one guide says food sources compete with cockroach baits, and a newer guide says current baits are extremely effective even when competing food is present, while sanitation still helps by opening up hiding places for inspection and control; so cleaning helps a treatment, and a kitchen does not have to be spotless for one to work

Before the visit, what UF/IFAS says to clean: UF/IFAS says to remove grease and oil by scrubbing with hot, soapy water before surfaces are treated; to keep toasters, microwaves, stoves, ovens and refrigerators free of crumbs and food debris and to clean the areas around them; and to discard unnecessary corrugated cardboard boxes at once, because cockroaches breed prolifically in them

briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: seasonal residents ask what to check for pests when they come back to a home that sat closed through the summer)
briefs.thesis: A Southwest Florida home that sat closed through the summer gives pests months without people. UF/IFAS says unoccupied homes are more susceptible to mildew, storm damage and pests, and that drains which dry out can let sewer gas and pests in. In the first days back, run water in every drain, check the pantry and the pet food, look for droppings before you sweep, look for termite pellets and mud tubes, empty anything that holds water, and keep away from any wasp nest. Termite signs, rodents and nests are jobs for a professional. No UF/IFAS checklist for the return exists that we could find, so these steps come from UF/IFAS and CDC pest guidance.
outline: The short answer: a house that sat closed through a Southwest Florida summer can come back with dry drain traps, pests in stored food, rodent droppings, termite signs, standing water and wasp nests; in the first days back, run water in every drain, check the pantry and the pet food, look for droppings before you sweep, look for termite signs, empty anything that holds water, and keep away from any nest; termite signs, rodents and nests are for a professional

Why pests find a closed house: the UF/IFAS guide to closing a seasonal home says Florida's environment creates the possibility of mildew growth, storm damage and pests, and that unoccupied homes are more susceptible to this damage; it says food particles and body oils left on towels, clothing and furnishings absorb water from the air and attract mildew, fungi and pests such as roaches and ants; its closing steps include throwing out cereals, crackers and pastas, storing no food in a garage or shed, removing standing water from the yard, and closing drain stoppers; one of its authors is a UF/IFAS Extension agent in Sarasota County; no UF/IFAS source we read gives a checklist for the return, so the steps below come from UF/IFAS and CDC pest guidance

Run water in every drain: the UF/IFAS closing guide says that if all moisture from drains evaporates, sewer gas and pests can enter the home through the drains; on the first day back, running water in each sink, tub, shower and toilet refills the traps (link /pest-control/cockroach-types-southwest-florida/)

Small flies on the bathroom walls: UF/IFAS says adult drain flies are commonly seen resting on the walls of bathrooms and showers near where they breed, and that the larvae feed on the film of wet organic material that can build up in drains; because drain flies fly poorly, the source is usually the closest drain; UF/IFAS says to confirm it by placing tape over the drain for 24 hours and then checking the tape for trapped flies; it says the simplest control is removing the organic material in the drain by hand, and that drain flies pose no health threat unless they emerge in large numbers, which is not common in homes; no source we read says that a dry drain causes drain flies (link /pest-control/get-rid-of-drain-flies/)

Leaks and storm damage: UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County says ants, cockroaches, silverfish and flies are some of the many pests that may be attracted to leaking water, and that dampwood termites and carpenter ants need moist wood to start their colonies; check under the sinks, around the water heater and at ceilings and window frames for leaks and water stains; a leak is a job for a plumber, a roofer or an air conditioning technician

The pantry and the pet food: UF/IFAS says most stored food pests are brought into homes in infested food, and that hardly any food item can escape being infested if it stays unused and exposed long enough; it says large populations may develop in unused or undisturbed food that was infested when it was bought, and that often the only sign is an infested, seldom-used item, or adults flying or crawling from the shelves; moths and beetles drawn to lights or windows may point to an infestation, and UF/IFAS says stored food pests are not a sign of uncleanliness; UF/IFAS says the first step is to find the source: inspect all susceptible foods, throw out badly infested items, vacuum the cabinets and shelves, and wash them with warm, soapy water; UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County says to throw out expired items, to wipe off any shelves where food may have spilled, and to store sugar, flour and grains in resealable bags or air-tight containers, and that the same goes for any pet food (link /pest-control/get-rid-of-pantry-moths/)

Check for droppings before you sweep: for cleanup, CDC says not to vacuum or sweep rodent urine, droppings or nesting materials, because this can put tiny droplets containing viruses into the air, to air out the space before cleaning, and to wear rubber or plastic gloves; for the full method, send readers to the CDC clean-up page; CDC says rodents may build nests in cars, trucks and campers, especially ones used infrequently, and to air out a vehicle that has been idle for an extended period before starting it; CDC says to contact a professional when there is evidence that rodents have reached the heating and cooling ventilation system; outside, UF/IFAS says rodents such as rats use overhanging or touching limbs as a highway into a home, and that a skirt of dead palm leaves is excellent rodent habitat (link /rodent-control/)

Termite signs to look for: UF/IFAS says drywood termite evidence includes six-sided pellets pushed out of the colony through kickholes about the size of a pen tip, and that drywood termites more commonly infest soffit and attic areas; it says mud tubes made of soil, termite feces and partly digested wood are strong evidence of subterranean termites, and to move items out of the garage and other storage areas from time to time to look for mud tubes; UF/IFAS says swarmers are a winged reproductive form, present only in spring and possibly fall, and notes that most people can see the waist on an ant, one of the features that separate swarming ants from swarming termites; UF/IFAS says termites generally require a pest management professional for control, that controlling an existing infestation is generally not a do-it-yourself project, and that its termite researchers will identify termites for free; no source we read says how to tell when wings were shed or whether pellets mean termites are active now, so leave that question to an inspection (link /termite/termite-swarmers/ and /termite-inspection/)

Standing water and mosquitoes: the UF/IFAS closing guide says to remove any standing water, such as buckets and bird baths, from the yard; UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County says containers stored outside can collect rainwater after a storm, that even something as small as a bottlecap can hold enough water for a mosquito to complete its life cycle, and to dump out containers and then flip them over or bring them inside; it says mosquitoes and midges come in through damaged screens and can make a porch or lanai very uncomfortable (link /mosquito/standing-water-checklist-swfl-patio/)

Wasp nests under the eaves: UF/IFAS describes a paper wasp nest as one circular comb of cells that opens downward, commonly found under eaves or window ledges, and says hornets and paper wasps nest in trees, shrubbery and under eaves; UF/IFAS says that if disturbed, hornets, yellow jackets and paper wasps will sting; do not knock down, spray or hose a nest; keep people and pets away from it and call a professional (link /pest-identifier/paper-wasp/)

What Waves does and does not do: recurring WaveGuard plans include unlimited callbacks between scheduled visits at no extra charge (link /waveguard-memberships/); anything that could be termites needs an inspection, not a guess (link /termite-inspection/); our rodent prep guide describes rodent work as a process with a trapping phase, a sealing phase and a verification phase, not a one-visit fix; Waves offers a nest service for paper wasps and yellow jackets; Waves does not repair plumbing, roofs, pools or air conditioning; to have the house looked at after a summer away, request a pest control quote (link /pest-control-services/); call to action: link "Request a Pest Control Quote" to /pest-control-quote/

briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: homeowners ask what to do about rats around the lanai, the pool equipment and the outdoor kitchen or grill)
briefs.thesis: Rats around a lanai, pool equipment or an outdoor kitchen in Southwest Florida can be roof rats or Norway rats. UF/IFAS calls the roof rat the primary suburban pest rat in Florida, and most of the rodent work Waves handles in this area is roof rats, but no source we read says which rat is most common around pool equipment. Rats come for food, water, shelter and warmth, so the first steps take those away: a clean grill, no pet food or birdseed left out, fallen fruit picked up, dead palm fronds trimmed, and gaps sealed with rodent-proof material. briefs.intent: informational (customer question, November 2026: tenants and landlords both call and ask which of them is responsible for pest control in a rental)
briefs.thesis: Florida law answers part of this question, and the lease answers the rest. Section 83.51 of the Florida Statutes says that, unless otherwise agreed in writing, the landlord of a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex shall make reasonable provisions for the extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms and bedbugs. That duty does not cover a rented single-family home or duplex, where the lease is the place to look. The tenant's own duties include keeping the unit clean and sanitary. This post reports what the statute and the state consumer agency say. It is not legal advice.
outline: The short answer: in an apartment or other multi-unit rental, Florida law puts the duty on the landlord to make reasonable provisions for the extermination of six named pests, unless the lease says otherwise in writing; in a rented single-family home or duplex, that duty does not apply and the lease decides; so read the lease first; this is a report of what the law says, not legal advice

What section 83.51 says for apartments: section 83.51 of the Florida Statutes says that, unless otherwise agreed in writing, the landlord of a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex shall, at all times during the tenancy, make reasonable provisions for the extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms and bedbugs; point out two things in that wording: it says make reasonable provisions for, not pay, and it opens with unless otherwise agreed in writing, so a written lease can change it

If you rent a house or a duplex: the extermination duty in that subsection is written for a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex; FDACS, the state consumer agency, says the landlord's obligations may be altered or modified in writing when renting a single-family dwelling or duplex, and it lists extermination under the heading for other dwellings such as apartments; so for a rented house or duplex the lease is the place to look; if the lease says nothing about pest control, the sources read for this post do not say who is responsible, and that is a question for an attorney or a legal aid office

What the tenant is responsible for: section 83.52 says the tenant shall keep the part of the premises that he or she occupies and uses clean and sanitary, remove all garbage from the dwelling unit in a clean and sanitary manner, and keep plumbing fixtures clean and sanitary and in repair; section 83.51 also says the landlord is not responsible to the tenant under that section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent

When a treatment means leaving the unit: these rules are in the extermination item of subsection (2)(a) of section 83.51, which opens with unless otherwise agreed in writing and covers the landlord of a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex; for that kind of unit, section 83.51 says that when the tenant must leave the premises for the extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent; the tenant gets 7 days' written notice, and the time out of the premises may not exceed 4 days; the statute does not state these rules for a single-family home or duplex, and it does not say which treatments require leaving
Pests the statute does not name: the list has six items; it does not name fleas, mosquitoes, spiders, wasps or lawn pests; for those, the lease is the place to look

What to do before you call anyone: read the lease and any addendum for a pest control clause; note which kind of unit you rent; write down what you have seen, where and when, and take photos; raise it with the landlord or property manager in writing and keep a copy; FDACS says the responsibilities of landlord and tenant may vary with the rental agreement and the type of rental unit, and describes its own page as a summary that is not legal advice

What Waves does and does not do: Waves does not interpret leases and cannot tell you which party is responsible under yours; a landlord or a tenant can request a pest control quote; after a visit Waves sends a service report that records what was found and what was done, and either party can share it with the other (link /pest-control/what-to-expect-pest-control-visit/ and /pest-control-services/); call to action: link "Request a Pest Control Quote" to /pest-control-quote/

briefs.working_title: Pre-Slab Termite Treatment: A Southwest Florida Builder's Guide
briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: a builder whose slab was pre-treated called to say the project was ready for the final termite treatment, and builders and owner-builders ask what the steps and the paperwork are)
briefs.thesis: On a new build or an addition in Florida, a preventive termite treatment is done by a licensed pest control company. Florida law requires the licensee to hold a permit for preventive termite treatment of new construction, with one exception for additions covered by a current termite treatment contract. UF/IFAS describes a pre-treatment as liquid termiticide applied to the soil under the foundation before it is poured and to the soil around the foundation perimeter. NC State Extension, writing for North Carolina, says a soil treatment is done in stages, and that the final phase comes after final grading and sometimes after landscaping, so that the treated soil is not disturbed. For a new single-family residence, Charlotte County's building department says a termite certificate from a commercial pesticide company is required before final inspections can be requested; for an addition or any other permit, the building department is the one to ask.
outline: The short answer: a licensed pest control company with a state permit does a preventive termite treatment on new construction, with one exception for additions covered by a current termite treatment contract; UF/IFAS says a pre-treatment is applied to the soil under the foundation before it is poured and to the soil around the foundation perimeter; NC State Extension, writing for North Carolina, says the final phase comes after final grading and sometimes after landscaping; anything that disturbs the treated soil may mean another treatment; your building department sets the paperwork and the timing, so ask it, and call the pest control company before the pour and again before the final

Who may do it: Florida Statutes section 482.0815 says a licensee must have a permit to perform preventive termite treatments for new construction, except for preventive termite treatments on additions to existing structures for which the licensee has a current termite treatment contract; section 482.021 defines new construction as the erection of a new building or the construction of an addition to an existing building, which encloses a space and requires a building permit under applicable building codes; so an addition counts as new construction, and the exception covers it when the company already has a current termite treatment contract on the existing home

Visit one, before the pour: UF/IFAS says that for pre-treatments, liquid termiticides are applied to the soil underneath the foundation before it is poured, as well as to soil around the perimeter of the foundation; NC State Extension says that for slab construction, including foundations, patios and garages, the entire soil or gravel surface is treated before the vapor barrier is installed and the slab is poured over it; it writes for North Carolina, so confirm the steps with your building department and your pest control company

What undoes the first visit: UF/IFAS says that if the treated soil around a home is disturbed, for instance by excavations for construction, digging by pets or wildlife, or a washing rain such as may be experienced during a hurricane, those areas may require another treatment; so plan the order on site: treat, cover, and keep digging off the treated soil

Visit two, after the grading is done: NC State Extension says a properly done soil treatment is not a one-time application; it is done in stages coordinated with all building activities from foundation construction through final grading of the soil around the building's exterior, and the final phase must be done after final grading and sometimes after landscaping is completed so that the treated soil is not disturbed; it writes for North Carolina, so ask your building department and your pest control company when the final treatment is due

If bait or a wood treatment is used: UF/IFAS says termite bait stations can be used as both new construction and remedial treatments; for a wood treatment, UF/IFAS says the builder calls the pest management professional when the framing elements are installed and construction is at the dried-in phase, and that framing and other wooden elements are sometimes moved or added after the treatment is done

The paperwork and the contract: for a new single-family residence, Charlotte County's building department says a termite certificate is required from a commercial pesticide company before final inspections can be requested; for an addition or any other permit type, and in every other county and city, the building department sets its own forms and timing, so ask it; Florida Statutes section 482.227 says a contract for treatment of wood-destroying organisms must specify on the first page in bold print that it is offered for repair and retreatment, for retreatment only, or that no warranty or guarantee is offered; UF/IFAS says some states, like Florida, allow companies to exclude Formosan and Asian subterranean termites from contract warranties, so read contracts carefully

After the home is sold: the same UF/IFAS guidance applies to the new owner: treated soil disturbed by digging, by pets or wildlife, or by a washing rain may require another treatment, so tell the buyer before new planting beds go in

briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: a homeowner found a long flat worm with a wide head in the yard after rain and asked what it is, whether it is dangerous and whether we treat for it)
briefs.thesis: A hammerhead worm in the yard is a land planarian that has been in the United States for more than a century. It is not a new invasion and not a reason for a yard treatment. UF/IFAS says it eats earthworms, slugs and insect larvae and reports no management method for it. Two university extension services say the one thing not to do is cut it up, because the pieces can regrow, and that a single worm should be picked up with gloves or tweezers, not bare hands. The post says what the sources know and do not know about its toxin, and it does not sell a treatment that does not exist.
outline: The short answer: it is a land planarian, often called a hammerhead worm; do not cut it or chop it; do not pick it up with bare hands; lift a single worm with gloved hands or tweezers into a sealed bag; no yard spray is reported to work against them, and Waves does not sell one

What a hammerhead worm looks like: UF/IFAS says the common species is recognized by its pale color, a dark line down the middle of its back, a dark patch at the neck and a wide half-moon-shaped head, and that it may reach about 30 cm, close to 12 inches; UF/IFAS says Florida species range from greenish-gray to brown with narrow dark stripes on the back; USDA lists the common names hammerhead worm, land planarian and shovel-headed garden worm; Pennsylvania State University Extension describes a second land planarian with a rounded head in place of the crescent-shaped one; UF/IFAS says a slime trail is telltale evidence of land planarians but might also mean slugs or snails (link /pest-control/gray-worms-southwest-florida-identification/ for other worms people find)

Where and when you find them: UF/IFAS says they prefer dark, cool, moist places under objects such as rocks, logs and debris or under shrubs, and come to the soil surface after heavy rain; they move and feed at night; UF/IFAS says land planarians are most abundant in spring and fall; that is why one tends to turn up in the open the morning after rain

Not a new arrival: UF/IFAS says the species is believed to be native to Indo-China and has been commonly found in American greenhouses since 1901; USDA lists 1891 as the date of its introduction to the United States, through the movement of infested plants and soil; UF/IFAS says land planarians spread through horticultural practices and potted plants in commerce and have been detected in natural habitats in Florida, and cites a Florida state report in which specimens were sent in for identification in almost every month of the year

What they eat, and what that means for a lawn or garden: UF/IFAS says land planarians devour earthworms, slugs, insect larvae and each other, and that two species have been reported as nuisances in earthworm rearing beds in the southern United States; UF/IFAS says that in greenhouses they are considered harmless to plants; USDA calls the hammerhead worm a predator of earthworms that could potentially impact agricultural, horticultural and natural ecosystems; NC State Extension says the actual impact on the environment is complicated and little understood; no source we read measures damage to a home lawn

Are they dangerous to people or pets: say what each source says and no more: UF/IFAS says other animals rarely eat land planarians because their surface secretions appear distasteful, if not toxic, and reports no disease transmission; NC State Extension says at least two hammerhead species, this one among them, produce tetrodotoxin, that there is very little information about the toxin's effects on humans, that the effect is likely minimal unless the worms are eaten in quantity, and that hands should be washed thoroughly after handling them; Pennsylvania State University Extension says there are no documented instances of pets or children being sickened by eating flatworms or of people being sickened by handling them, and advises gloves or immediate hand washing because the worms may be irritating to the eyes or mouth; if a child or a pet eats one and seems unwell, call a doctor or a veterinarian

What to do when you find one: do not cut it: UF/IFAS says these worms reproduce mainly by fragmentation and that a broken-off piece begins to form a head within seven to 10 days; NC State Extension says first and foremost not to cut up the worms, because cut fragments can generate a new worm from each section, and Pennsylvania State University Extension says cutting them into pieces just creates more; NC State Extension says a worm picked up with tweezers or gloved hands can be killed in rubbing alcohol or put in a bag and frozen; then wash your hands

Why there is no yard treatment: UF/IFAS lists no management method for land planarians; NC State Extension says eradication from a lawn and landscape can be difficult, if not impossible, and Pennsylvania State University Extension says management in the landscape is difficult to impossible; so removing the single worms you see is the practical step, and a pesticide bought for them is money spent on something no cited source reports to work

What Waves does and does not do: Waves does not sell a treatment for hammerhead worms, because none is established; if you are not sure what you found, our pest identifier page takes a photo (link /pest-identifier/), and the pest library covers the yard and home pests we do treat (link /pest-library/); for those, request a pest control quote; call to action: link "Request a Pest Control Quote" to /pest-control-quote/

briefs.working_title: Plug-In Repellers, Bug Bombs and Glue Traps: Do They Work?
briefs.primary_kw: do plug in pest repellers work
secondary_kws: do sticky traps work for roaches
briefs.intent: informational (customer question, November 2026: customers ask whether the plug-in repellers, bug bombs and glue traps sold in stores work, often after trying one)
briefs.thesis: The three store-bought shortcuts customers ask about most do not hold up the way their packages suggest. EPA does not review plug-in repellers before they are sold, and in a 2003 case the FTC challenged a seller's claims and required scientific proof for them. Bug bombs carry fire and illness risks that EPA and CDC document, and EPA says the fog kills only the pests it contacts. Sticky traps are useful for one job: UF/IFAS says they monitor cockroaches and can reduce their numbers. CDC says not to use glue traps for rodents.
outline: The short answer: plug-in repellers: EPA does not review them before sale, and no agency or university source we read shows they control household pests; bug bombs: they reach only the insects the fog touches, and EPA and CDC document fire and illness risks; sticky traps: good for finding out where cockroaches are and how many there are; for rodents, CDC says not to use glue traps

Plug-in repellers, what EPA says: EPA treats products that claim to control pests by electromagnetic or electrical means, such as ultrasonic insect and rodent repellers, as devices, not pesticides, when no pesticide is sold with them; for devices there is no required premarket review, and federal pesticide law does not require them to be registered; device makers and sellers generally do not submit their claims or their efficacy and safety data to EPA before they sell; an EPA establishment number on the package does not mean EPA reviewed the product for safety or efficacy

Plug-in repellers and an FTC case: in a 2003 case, the FTC's complaint against a seller of electromagnetic and ultrasonic pest control devices alleged that claims such as ultrasonic devices driving away mice, rats, spiders and other insects were unsubstantiated, and the proposed order barred such claims unless the seller had competent and reliable scientific evidence; this was a proposed consent agreement, not a finding that no device can work (link /mosquito/mosquito-repellents/)

Bug bombs, where the fog does not reach: EPA says the pesticide in a total release fogger must contact the pest to kill it, and that pests hiding in cracks and crevices the material does not reach will not be killed; insects that live in wall voids, behind appliances and in cracks are the ones a fog does not touch

Bug bombs, the risks EPA and CDC document: EPA says the aerosol propellants in these foggers typically are flammable, so improper use may cause a fire or explosion, and accidents are most likely when a large amount of fogger material reaches a flame, a pilot light or a spark from an appliance that cycles on and off; EPA's own advice is to use fogging devices only when absolutely necessary; a CDC report counted 3,222 fogger-related illness cases in 10 states from 2007 to 2015, 658 of them in Florida, and found that the two most commonly reported causes were not leaving during the application and going back in too early

Sticky traps: UF/IFAS says sticky traps can be used to monitor German cockroaches or to reduce their population; that makes them a tool for seeing where activity is and whether it is going down; our prep guide for German cockroach treatments asks customers to leave the sticky monitors in place (link /pest-control/get-rid-of-german-cockroaches/)

Glue traps and rodents: CDC says not to use glue traps or live traps for rodents, because these traps can scare the rodents and cause them to urinate, which can increase your chance of getting sick; our post on mice covers what to do instead (link /pest-control/get-rid-of-mice/)

What works better than a shortcut: EPA says that learning about the pests you have and the options for controlling them is the first step; EPA then lists removing sources of food, water and shelter, storing food in sealed containers, fixing leaks, getting rid of clutter such as stacks of newspapers and cardboard, and closing off places where pests can enter and hide

briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: homeowners ask what to do when wasps or bees come out of an outlet, a bathroom fan, a vent or a gap in a wall)
briefs.thesis: Wasps or bees coming out of an outlet, a fan grille or a gap in a wall may have a nest somewhere behind it; leave the cover in place and have a professional find the nest. UF/IFAS says that when a nest is large or hard to approach, for example within the walls of a house, the safest procedure is to hire a pest control operator. Do not seal, spray or open the hole: two university extension services warn that plugging a hidden yellowjacket nest or spraying into it can send the insects into the home, and our pest identifier says sealing a honey bee wall colony traps the bees and can leak honey into the wall. Bees and wasps need different handling, so the first step is to tell them apart from a distance.
outline: The short answer: keep people and pets away from the opening, do not seal it, spray it or take off the cover, note from a distance whether the insects are bees or wasps, and have a professional find the nest; for honey bees, the answer is removal of the colony, not a plugged hole

What may be behind the opening: insects that come out of an outlet, a bath fan grille or a gap in a soffit may be nesting somewhere behind it, and no source we read says which insect it is or where the nest is; MedlinePlus, a federal medical encyclopedia, says hornets and wasps build their large nests in trees or bushes as well as in manmade structures such as roof overhangs, house walls and attics; UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County says social wasps may nest near or on human structures; UF/IFAS records above-ground yellowjacket nests between the sidings of a home and calls such locations unusual; the UF/IFAS stinging insect guide lists wall voids as a nest site for honey bees; no source we read names outlets, bath fans or utility boxes, so say that plainly

Bees or wasps: our pest identifier says the signs of a honey bee wall colony are steady bee traffic in and out of one gap in a soffit, wall or meter box, a low hum from the wall on warm afternoons, and activity that goes on for weeks; UF/IFAS says Florida has two yellowjacket species, that their colonies hold hundreds to thousands of insects, and that each nest is a series of horizontal combs inside a paper envelope; UF/IFAS says yellow jackets usually nest in the ground but sometimes above it; UF/IFAS describes a paper wasp nest as one circular comb of cells that opens downward, commonly under eaves or window ledges; UF/IFAS says mud daubers nest under eaves, porch roofs or similar sheltered areas (link /pest-identifier/honey-bee-wall-colony/, /pest-identifier/yellowjacket/ and /pest-identifier/paper-wasp/)

Do not seal, spray or open it: Pennsylvania State University Extension says never to try to control yellowjackets in a wall by plugging the opening, because they can chew through the interior drywall and enter the home; the University of Minnesota says not to seal a nest opening until all of the yellowjackets are dead, and that an aerosol spray can send them looking for another exit, which often leads them into the home; both write for their own states; our pest identifier says never to seal the entrance of a honey bee wall colony while bees are active, because that traps them and can leak honey into the wall; UF/IFAS says hornets, yellow jackets and paper wasps will sting if disturbed, and that yellowjackets may sting as often as they find a target; MedlinePlus says disturbing a nest puts you at risk of stings, so leave the outlet cover and the fan grille in place

Who should handle a nest in a wall: UF/IFAS says that when a nest is large or hard to approach, for example within the walls of a house, the safest procedure is to hire a pest control operator to eliminate the colony; for honey bees, our pest identifier says a wall colony needs bee-friendly removal, with the comb taken out and the cavity cleaned, not just the hole plugged (link /pest-control/honeybee-vs-yellow-jacket/)

When a sting is an emergency: NIOSH, part of CDC, says people who are allergic to venom may have anaphylaxis, a severe and potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that requires immediate emergency care; MedlinePlus says to call 911 if someone with a sting has trouble breathing, wheezing or shortness of breath, swelling anywhere on the face or in the mouth, throat tightness or difficulty swallowing, feels weak, or turns blue; for any other reaction, see a doctor

briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: customers arrive with a pest name that a photo app or an AI chat tool gave them, and the name turns out to be wrong)
briefs.thesis: A pest name from a photo app or an AI chat tool is a first guess, not an identification, and that includes the photo tool on our own website. EPA and UF/IFAS both say that correct identification comes before any control decision, and look-alikes such as flying ants and termite swarmers are told apart by their wings, waist and antennae. Florida residents have expert help close by: the county UF/IFAS Extension office, the UF Insect ID Lab and the UF termite identification team. Even the UF lab says it cannot guarantee an identification made from a photo. So confirm the name before you treat, or pay for a treatment.
outline: The short answer: use the app or chat answer to narrow it down, then confirm it before you spend money or apply anything; keep the insect, take clear photos, and ask a person who can look at the insect or the evidence: your county UF/IFAS Extension office, the UF Insect ID Lab, or a licensed pest control technician

Why you need the right name first: EPA says integrated pest management programs identify pests accurately so that appropriate control decisions can be made, and that monitoring and identification removes the possibility that pesticides will be used when they are not really needed or that the wrong kind of pesticide will be used; UF/IFAS says it is very important to correctly identify the insect before deciding which control measures to take, or deciding if control is even needed

What UF/IFAS says about AI answers: a UF/IFAS page written about gardening questions says the response an AI chat tool formulates may not come from qualified organizations or experts and can be inaccurate and misleading, because these programs search many sources without telling commercially driven content from scientific information; the same page says AI answers can help narrow down options but should still be verified, and tells readers to confirm facts with UF/IFAS publications and the local county Extension office; no university or government source we read measures how often photo apps or chat tools name an insect wrong, so this post gives no accuracy figure

Flying ants or termite swarmers: UF/IFAS says a winged ant has elbowed antennae, a narrow waist and hind wings smaller than its front wings, while a winged termite has front and hind wings of equal size and a broad waist; UF/IFAS says it is critical that a termite sample be identified to species before seeking treatment options, and that Florida has 20 established termite species (link /termite/bugs-that-look-like-termites/)

Even experts limit what a photo can prove: the UF Insect ID Lab says it can provide tentative diagnostic services by email but cannot guarantee the accuracy of photo identification; UF/IFAS says that, depending on the sample, only a genus, family or order level identification may be possible, and that for many insects a species identification can only be made from the adult stage; so a confident species name from one phone photo deserves a second look

How to take a photo and keep a specimen that someone can use: UF/IFAS guidance for digital diagnosis says images should include an entire view as well as close-up views of the features that make identification possible; UF/IFAS says the quality of the sample affects the quality of the identification and that more specimens are generally better; most insects can be killed in a freezer or in a vial of ordinary rubbing alcohol; UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County says to keep specimens in the refrigerator or freezer until you can bring them in, because a specimen left outdoors or in the car becomes brittle and extremely difficult to identify, and that most adult insects longer than 5 mm can go in a zipper-style plastic bag

briefs.intent: informational how-to (customer question, November 2026: homeowners about to list a house ask for a single weed spray so the lawn looks good for the listing and showings)
briefs.thesis: One weed spray a few days before the listing photos will not give a seller a clean lawn. UF/IFAS says systemic herbicides can take 7 to 10 days or longer to show symptoms, that repeat applications are usually necessary, and that weeds fill gaps in a weakened lawn rather than cause them. Dead patches of St. Augustinegrass do not come back from seed: UF/IFAS says the grass is established only from sod, plugs or sprigs. A seller who books weed control weeks ahead, so that young weeds are treated in the right weather with time for a second application, and who fixes the thin spots, has the better-looking lawn on listing day.
outline: The short answer: a weed spray works over days and weeks, not overnight, and stubborn weeds often need a second application; dead or bare patches need sod or plugs; so book weed control weeks before the listing date, not days, and plan for the thin spots as well as the weeds

How fast a weed spray works: UF/IFAS says it may take 7 to 10 days or longer for symptoms to appear after a systemic herbicide is applied, and that systemic herbicides generally kill plants over a period of days; what we tell our own lawn customers is that weeds yellow and wilt over 1 to 2 weeks and that stubborn perennials may need a second pass; UF/IFAS says repeat applications at the interval on the product label are usually necessary for satisfactory weed control

Heat, drought and young weeds: UF/IFAS says a weed spray works less well when the weed is under drought or cold stress, has begun to produce seeds, or is mowed before the product has had several days to work, and that rain or irrigation that washes it off the leaves too early reduces its effect; for St. Augustinegrass, UF/IFAS says these products should not be applied when the lawn is under moisture stress or when air temperatures exceed 85 degrees F; UF/IFAS also says younger weeds are easier to control, while mature weeds need high rates that raise the risk of injuring the lawn

Weed control before and after weeds come up: UF/IFAS says preemergence herbicides are applied before weed seeds germinate and have little or no effect on weeds that have already come up, and that postemergence herbicides act on weeds that are already up; so weeds that are already up call for a postemergence product, and a preemergence product works only on seeds that have not come up yet; ask the lawn company which one fits your weeds and your listing date; UF/IFAS gives late October to early November for winter weeds in central and south Florida, and February 1 in south Florida and February 15 in central Florida for spring, as general timing rules (link /lawn-care/pre-emergent-weed-control-lakewood-ranch-fl/ and /lawn-care/post-emergent-herbicides-lakewood-ranch-fl/)

Why the weeds are there, and what fixes the gaps: UF/IFAS says the presence of weeds is a result of a weakened lawn, not the cause of it, and that weeds do not create a void, they fill one; healthy, thick turf shades the soil so weed seeds do not get sunlight; for St. Augustinegrass, the most common lawn grass in Florida, UF/IFAS says standard varieties mowed with a rotary mower should be kept at 3.5 to 4 inches, and that mowing too low badly stresses the lawn and leaves it open to weeds (link /lawn-care/mowing-height-by-grass-type/ and /lawn-care/types-of-weeds-bradenton-fl/)
